source_location: Paper p. 10, Part II: The question; research/source/expanded_lifetime_model.py SCENARIOS and simulate()
source_text: Two otherwise identical Gauteng couples each receive R30,000 plus R20,000 in monthly disposable income; one consolidates at 25 and the other at 35; both are followed to 75.
social_wording: The model compares two otherwise identical Gauteng couples with R50,000 monthly disposable income who combine households at 25 or 35.
qualifier: Hypothetical counterfactual; both relationships remain intact; ages 25-75; monthly income is after tax and payroll deductions.

source_location: Paper p. 11, The starting Gauteng budget; research/source/expanded_lifetime_model.py Average case
source_text: At age 25 the average case costs R44,800 monthly for two homes and R36,300 for one shared home, releasing R8,500.
social_wording: Under the central assumptions, sharing one home releases R8,500 a month at age 25.
qualifier: Average scenario; constant 2026 rand; urban employed middle-income Gauteng renter; not an estimate for the average Gauteng household.

source_location: Paper pp. 14-15, Average case table; expanded_lifetime_model.py Average case age-35 milestones
source_text: At 35 the Early couple has R2.260 million and the Later couple R1.072 million, a R1.188 million lead including pension saving.
social_wording: By age 35, modeled combined net worth is R2.260m versus R1.072m, a R1.188m head start.
qualifier: Average scenario; combined household net worth; rounded; constant 2026 rand.

source_location: Paper p. 15, Average case table; expanded_lifetime_model.py Average case age-75 milestones
source_text: At 75 the Early couple has R13.833 million and the Later couple R9.861 million, a R3.972 million lead.
social_wording: At age 75, the central model produces R13.833m versus R9.861m in combined household wealth, a R3.972m gap.
qualifier: Average scenario; combined household net worth; constant 2026 rand; not a forecast.

source_location: Paper p. 16, The comparison in one table; expanded_lifetime_model.py age-75 gaps
source_text: The age-75 advantage is R11.287 million in the best case, R3.972 million in the average case and R1.882 million in the worst case.
social_wording: Across the three modeled paths, moving in at 25 rather than 35 leaves the household R1.9m-R11.3m ahead at 75.
qualifier: Constant 2026 rand; combined household outcome; the worst-case advantage is a smaller unfunded shortfall, not positive wealth; not a forecast.

source_location: Paper p. 17, Why the difference keeps growing after both couples move in
source_text: After 35 the households have the same living arrangement; the remaining gap changes through investment returns or deficit-financing costs.
social_wording: The direct saving creates a balance-sheet head start that can compound through returns or protection from expensive negative balances.
qualifier: Model mechanism; depends on the model's return, saving and financing-cost assumptions.

source_location: Paper p. 18, What still cannot be reduced to a credible rand value
source_text: The simulation assumes every available surplus is invested; real households may spend some on lifestyle improvements.
social_wording: The modeled wealth gap assumes available surplus is invested.
qualifier: The model omits monetised relationship quality, privacy, safety and actual separation costs.

source_location: Paper pp. 18-19, The household and the individuals
source_text: The results describe combined household wealth and do not prove that both people own half or have equal access.
social_wording: Combined household wealth is not evidence that each partner owns or controls half.
qualifier: No individual asset, liability, unpaid-work or control ledger is modeled.

source_location: Paper pp. 13-16, Three possible lives and scenario results
source_text: Best, average and worst cases test whether the cohabitation advantage survives different assumptions; they do not select or predict one future.
social_wording: The R1.9m-R11.3m range is a scenario result, not a forecast.
qualifier: Conditional on stated income, cost, return, family, shock and retirement assumptions.

source_location: Paper pp. 15-16, Worst case and comparison table; research/source/expanded_lifetime_model.py Worst case age-75 milestones
source_text: At 75 the Early household has a R16.346 million funding shortfall and the Later household a R18.228 million shortfall, leaving the Early path R1.882 million ahead.
social_wording: In the worst-case model, moving in at 25 leaves the age-75 funding shortfall R1.882m smaller but does not eliminate it.
qualifier: Worst-case scenario; constant 2026 rand; negative values are unfunded continuation of the modelled lifestyle, not literal lender debt.

source_location: Paper p. 14, Best case; research/source/expanded_lifetime_model.py Best case outputs
source_text: The Early household avoids R1.261 million in living costs and finishes R11.287 million ahead at 75 in the best case.
social_wording: In the favourable model, R1.261m of avoided living costs becomes an R11.287m age-75 wealth lead through compounding.
qualifier: Best-case scenario; combined household wealth; constant 2026 rand; favourable outcome, not a forecast or promise.

source_location: Paper p. 7, The welfare-GDP paradox; p. 19, What this means outside the household
source_text: An avoided second rent can improve household welfare while reducing measured market consumption; GDP does not count the avoided transaction as positive output.
social_wording: One rent avoided can improve household finances even while measured consumption falls.
qualifier: Conceptual mechanism; the wider GDP effect depends on how released income and resources are redirected.

source_location: Paper pp. 10 and 19, The question and What this means outside the household
source_text: For ten years the Later couple supports two rental units and duplicated household infrastructure while the Early couple supports one larger unit.
social_wording: Household formation changes housing demand even when population is unchanged.
qualifier: Modelled two-couple comparison; macro effects are conditional if many similar households make the same choice.

source_text: The advantage disappears or reverses if shared housing is almost as expensive as two homes, the saving is entirely consumed, personal or career costs are large, or separation costs exceed the accumulated benefit.
social_wording: The modelled financial advantage is conditional and can reverse when key assumptions fail.
qualifier: Sensitivity statement, not a quantified threshold; relationship quality and separation are not numerically modelled.
